children: The revised motor vehicle rules recognise E100 for compatible flex-fuel vehicles as India expands its ethanol adoption programme

India has amended its motor vehicle rules to formally recognise E100 ethanol fuel for compatible flex-fuel vehicles, creating a regulatory framework for vehicles capable of running on higher ethanol blends.

The Ministry of Road Transport and Highways amended the Central Motor Vehicles Rules, 1989, to include E100 alongside E85 in provisions governing emission standards and vehicle testing. The changes were notified in the Official Gazette on 23 October.
E100 Use Limited To Compatible Vehicles

E100 refers to fuel containing 100 per cent ethanol, while E85 contains 85 per cent ethanol. Flex-fuel vehicles are designed to operate on different petrol-ethanol blends, depending on their specifications.
Under the revised rules, E85 and E100 are intended for vehicles specifically designed and certified by original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) to use these fuels.

The amendment does not mean conventional petrol vehicles can switch to E100. Vehicles designed for regular petrol or E20 fuel are not automatically compatible with higher ethanol blends. Owners would need vehicles specifically engineered for such fuels.
The regulatory change provides a framework for manufacturers looking to develop and introduce vehicles capable of running on higher ethanol concentrations.

Maruti Suzuki India has showcased a flex-fuel version of the Wagon R designed to operate on ethanol-petrol blends ranging from E20 to E100. Automakers have been exploring flex-fuel technology as India expands its ethanol-blending programme.

However, the notification does not by itself guarantee the immediate availability of E100 at fuel stations or the widespread launch of compatible vehicles. Adoption will depend on vehicle availability, fuel distribution and supporting infrastructure.
Push To Reduce Oil Import Dependence
The move supports India's efforts to increase the use of domestically produced ethanol in transport and reduce dependence on imported crude oil.

India has expanded ethanol blending in petrol, with E20 fuel containing 20 per cent ethanol becoming an important part of its alternative-fuel strategy. Higher ethanol blends could create additional demand for biofuels and reduce petrol consumption in compatible vehicles.
However, wider adoption will depend on the economics of ethanol production, vehicle costs and the availability of suitable fuel infrastructure.

The amendment formally recognises E100 within India's vehicle regulatory framework, but its commercial impact will depend on how quickly manufacturers and fuel suppliers develop the supporting ecosystem.
